scholaris.title: Scholaris — the honest curve
scholaris.text: Welcome to Scholaris. This is the planet of the honest curve. Shyam finished Class Ten in 2019 with eighty-eight percent, and Class Twelve in 2021 with eighty-five percent in science. His bachelor's in Computer Applications, from Gauhati University, ended in 2024 with a seven point oh five CGPA. That number matters, because of what came next. At the joint MCA program of IIT Patna and IIIT Ranchi, his first semester came in at nine point six. His second, at nine point eight. Nothing magical happened in between. He learned how to learn: build the project, watch it break, find out why. Along the way he picked up Oracle certifications in generative AI and DevOps, and a national rank two at the IISc Pravega machine-learning challenge. The curve is the point. It only goes one way when you keep showing up.

stillwater.title: Stillwater — a hundred lanterns
stillwater.text: This is Stillwater, the service planet. For a year and a half, Shyam volunteered as a software engineer for the Vipassana Research Institute, and grew into the technical lead of its inventory management system. Today that system keeps books and materials moving for more than one hundred meditation centres around the world. It is built in TypeScript, React and Supabase, with a three-tier semantic search: stored answers first, then content, then metadata, each with its own confidence threshold, so the system can say: I'm not sure. He also contributed to a six-engine OCR platform for English and Hindi, a retrieval platform called Pala with role-based access, and audio fingerprinting with CLAP embeddings and Milvus. No one was paying for this. That is exactly why it had to keep working after the demo.

wordwatch.title: Crownfall — the audit trail
wordwatch.text: You are on Crownfall, the compliance planet. For six months, Shyam worked as a senior software engineer at Wordwatch, an enterprise compliance platform from the United Kingdom, on a React and TypeScript front end and C sharp dot NET services. In that time he shipped more than ninety pull requests and a hundred and fifty commits across four repositories. He built automatic risk-flag detection for transcription, instant-message and SMS ingest, and the access control around it. He delivered Share Saved Search end to end. And when a production five-hundred error appeared in the share flow, he fixed it, then wrote the regression tests so it would stay fixed. He also worked on the monitoring stack: Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, Elasticsearch and RabbitMQ. In regulated software, the audit trail is the product.

foundry.title: Foundry — impressive first, wrong second
foundry.text: Welcome to the Foundry, where things get built and then tested until they break. Nexus Prime is an agentic incident responder. On a hundred and fifty incidents it reached ninety percent top-one accuracy, but it also hallucinated eight percent of the time, until a safety validator brought that down to one point two. Median diagnosis time fell from forty-eight minutes to six seconds, and the work became a paper accepted at IEEE COMPSAC 2026. AURA won the AWS Global Vibe hackathon and earned ten thousand dollars of support to go to production. A S T R A repairs vulnerable code offline, for air-gapped networks, benchmarked on a hundred and four CVE fix pairs, because no model should approve its own patch. And Vayu, a national top nine at ISRO's hackathon, forecasts weather from forty-five years of data. Every one of these was impressive first, and wrong somewhere second.

meridian.title: Meridian — say the baseline
meridian.text: This is Meridian, the observatory. Shyam's research is applied AI, done as an independent researcher. His paper on agentic incident response, with a safety validator in the loop, was accepted at IEEE COMPSAC 2026. The rule on this planet is simple: say the baseline out loud before you say the accuracy. You can see it in the trading work too. At IMC Prosperity 4, against more than eighteen thousand teams, he finished at world rank three hundred thirty-two overall, with world rank eighteen in round four and thirty-two in round five. On Kaggle, as shyam three one four one five, he has published datasets, notebooks and benchmarks. And across more than nine hackathon wins and podiums, from AWS to IISc Bengaluru, IIT Bombay and a pitch stage in Mumbai, the lesson stayed the same: measure it, or it didn't happen.

breath.title: One Breath — the test I'd run first
breath.text: You've reached One Breath, the launch pad. This world is a proposal, not a result. If Shyam joined Wispr Flow, this is the first experiment he would run. Fourteen days in Bangalore, with students, early-career operators and developers who choose to opt in. The idea: if a first voice workflow can be finished in a single breath, and it connects to a real job to be done, people will come back to it without being prompted. The north star is repeat activation, a second use within seven days. The kill condition is just as clear: if fewer than twenty percent return by day ten, stop and redesign. The three thousand dollar field kit pays participants fairly, covers translation and accessibility, and keeps consent ahead of every public lesson. Speaking is the fastest way to think. The question is whether it becomes a habit.
